learning_objective: 🎯 Explore the core pillars of Indian society: Caste, Tribe, and Family, and discover how they adapt and change in the modern world!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Caste (Jati) is determined by birth. It enforces rules about marriage (endogamy), food sharing, occupational specialization, and is arranged in a hierarchy of purity and pollution.
Varna is a broad, ancient 4-tier theoretical model (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra). Jati is the complex, real-world system of thousands of localized endogamous groups.
Communities historically outside the caste system, deeply connected to forests and land. They are classified by traits (language, race) and acquired traits (mode of livelihood).
The family is a vital social institution. While the traditional 'joint family' is changing due to urbanization, kinship networks remain crucial in Indian society.

fun_activity.title: 🌳 The Kinship Tree
fun_activity.instructions: Draw a family tree spanning three generations. Ask your parents what specific roles different relatives (like maternal uncle vs paternal uncle) play in family rituals. Note how these roles differ based on your regional culture!

exam_tips: 📌 Always highlight M.N. Srinivas's concept of 'Sanskritisation' when discussing how lower castes attempt upward mobility.
📌 Distinguish between the 'integrationist' and 'isolationist' debates regarding tribal assimilation in post-independence India.
📌 Remember that colonialism heavily formalized the caste system through the Census.
quick_recap: ⭐ The caste system dictates both who you can marry (endogamy) and traditionally what job you do.
⭐ Colonial land settlements and forest laws severely disrupted the lives of tribal communities.
⭐ Despite urbanization, the caste system hasn't vanished; it has adapted into a modern political and social identity.
